endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Additional considerations include whether end users and patients will have access to the same documentation as stakeholders involved in technical aspects of implementation and piloting, and whether those decisions adequately account for the needs of both patients and end users.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Supporting resources such as AI fact sheets, model cards (such as the CHAI Applied Model Card), or solution documentation should remain accessible to staff between formal training cycles for self-directed review, if interested.

endorsements.title: Responsible Use of AI in Healthcare (RUAIH) guidance
endorsements.issuer: The Joint Commission and Coalition for Health AI
endorsements.quote: Staff and providers should know where to gain access to relevant information about the AI tool and its use and what the organization’s AI policies and procedures are.

evidence.title: "I worry we'll blow right by it:" Barriers to Uptake of the STRATIFY-CDS for Acute Heart Failure
evidence.outcome: Availability of risk model and evidence information to clinicians at point of use
evidence.effect: When the recommendation mismatched clinical gestalt, participants needed more information about the risk model and evidence, which was not readily available; this lowered perceived utility.
evidence.quote: When there was mismatch, perceived utility was lower, and participants needed more information about the risk model and supporting evidence, which were not readily available.

commentary.bottom_line: Three frameworks endorse keeping model documentation available to clinicians at the moment of use, but no study has tested whether doing so reduces inappropriate use. One qualitative study of 10 emergency department clinicians found that model and evidence information was not readily available when a recommendation conflicted with clinical judgment, and this lowered the tool's perceived utility.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The only study is a qualitative interview study of 10 emergency department clinicians at a single deployment site in the United States. It suggests the access gap exists. It cannot show that accessible documentation changes clinician behavior or patient outcomes.

Clinicians in the hazard study looked for model and evidence information when a risk score disagreed with their clinical gestalt. That moment is when an inappropriate acceptance or override may occur, and the information was not readily available. No study has tested whether documentation at the point of use helps clinicians catch model errors before they reach patients.

Participants reported that missing model information lowered the tool's perceived utility. This suggests that how documentation is delivered may affect adoption as well as correct use. No study has measured how often clinicians open embedded model cards, how much time retrieval adds, or which formats clinicians can use during a busy encounter.

The hazard study does not report on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, and no study tests the practice in any population. The CHAI guide asks whether patients can see the same documentation as technical staff. No evidence shows how plain-language documentation works for patients with limited literacy or limited English proficiency.

The CHAI guide places patient access to documentation alongside clinician access. Patients may benefit indirectly when clinicians can check what a tool was designed to do before acting on its output. No study reports patient views on documentation access or measures its effect on patient trust.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares point-of-use documentation, such as a model card linked within the electronic health record at the time of the alert, against usual access through intranet or training materials. Such a study should measure how often clinicians access the documentation, whether their acceptance and override decisions become more appropriate, how much time retrieval adds, and whether results hold across emergency, inpatient, and outpatient settings, including safety-net hospitals.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tests the practice, and the single hazard study of 10 emergency department clinicians does not describe whether its setting served Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems therefore have no evidence on whether documentation access works the same way for clinicians caring for these populations, or on how patient-facing documentation should be written for them.
